extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic (dramatic) poems: structuring action, choosing subject-matter, integrating chorus, provoking passions, and handling diction/pronunciation according to classical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy is vicious when it is episodical
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tragedy is vitious when it hath Episodes which are not well united with the principal Action; it is also vicious when it has too many (how proper soever they may be).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting loosely related episodes or an excess of episodes. Every episode should be tightly united to the main action; superfluous episodes harm the unity and effectiveness of the tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat large subjects in parts (do not compress whole histories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put the whole history (e.g., all the destruction of Troy) into one piece; manage large subjects in parts rather than attempting the entire subject at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single part or incident of a large subject sufficient to make one entire, perfect tragedy (example: Euripides' Medea uses only the revenge episode). Trying to include every particular of a great event leads to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose one part of the subject to be the focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should make use of one part of a subject (not all its misfortunes) to form the plot — as in Medea where the revenge is the single part used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the plot on a single contiguous episode or aspect of the story that yields a coherent beginning, middle, and end; avoid bundling multiple distinct misfortunes into one play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiplicity of fables / multiple plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not compose a tragedy as an 'Epick Complication' with many separate fables; multiplicity of fables undermines success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single, unified action rather than several imbricated or competing plots. One or two good parts do not suffice if the whole is disunited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and verisimilitude (drama founded on probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Dramatic Poem is always founded on Probability and would rather admit a likely fiction than an unlikely truth; it requires the common and ordinary sort of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid events that directly shock verisimilitude. Extraordinary incidents may be used sparingly but should not violate the audience's sense of what is plausible within the world of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character composition suited to plot type (simple vs complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple pieces (without peripeties) tragic and agreeable subjects may feature wicked persons whose other qualities make their fall plausible; in complex (regular) plots, principal persons should be neither wholly good nor wholly wicked (or rather more good than bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the moral makeup of principal characters to the plot form: simple, continuous misery may tolerate more clearly wicked protagonists if they retain qualities that generate pity/interest; complex plots need more morally mixed protagonists to sustain probability and ethical nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must be integrated and take part in the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus must take the part of an actor so that it makes one part of the whole and contributes to the advancement of the action; it lays the foundation of the probability of the tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the Chorus as an interested group drawn from the action's world (their presence must be plausible). The Chorus should work with the actors toward the same end, not be a detached spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus duties: sing only what agrees with the subject and advances the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus ought to sing nothing but what is agreeable to the subject, and concurs to the advancement of the action; it should show the intervals of the acts and tend to the same end as the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interstitial songs to comment on, reflect upon, or propel the action. Avoid extraneous songs that do not relate to the subject or move the plot forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use foreign or borrowed choruses (avoid adventitious songs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserted songs taken from elsewhere or borrowed for convenience (the practice attributed to Agathon) are condemned — such choruses are not drawn from the subject and could be transferred to any play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose Chorus material specifically for the play's subject; do not paste in generic or borrowed songs/recitations that could fit any tragedy, since they undermine unity and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid musical interludes/instrumental airs that disrupt unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern instrumental airs (e.g., violins) that separate acts are worse than a foreign Chorus because they break the continuity of the action and prevent the tragedy from being one consistent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer choral songs that maintain thematic continuity; avoid lengthy instrumental interludes that leave the audience disconnected from the action and harm unity of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus performance form: one speaker and appropriate restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus could not be silent in the course of the acts, but all speaking together would create confusion; therefore one person (a spokesperson) speaks for the Chorus and the Chorus performs its duties with decorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize choral speech so a single chorus-voice represents the group's stance; avoid crowd-speech that obscures principal actors and confuses the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets should draw on rhetorical forms for sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments (matter of discourse that proves, refutes, excites passions like pity, anger, fear) are similar to what orators use; poets ought to make use of the same forms and common rhetorical resources to render things pityful, terrible, probable, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical techniques and established argumentative/practical topoi to shape speeches and provoke intended passions; treat sentiment construction as a rhetorical task adapted to poetic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poet's material from orator's; poets may select inherently moving subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subjects are naturally affecting without art (e.g., histories of Oedipus, Ajax); poets choose such subjects and so sometimes need less rhetorical artifice than orators, who must handle all sorts of matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject itself is naturally moving, rely on its intrinsic power; when it is not, deploy rhetorical shaping to make it affective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction divided: elocution vs action (pronunciation & gesture belong to actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction has a part for show and the stage — pronunciation and gesture — but these properly concern actors/comedians (a separate art). The poet's responsibility is not the actor's pronunciation or gesture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the poet's craft on language and sentiment; accept that delivery (voice, gesture, stagecraft) is the actor's domain and faults there should not be imputed to the poem itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors must manage voice, tone, gesture, and harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronunciation depends on knowledge of how to use every passion in the voice: rising/falling tones, acute/grave/circumflex, combined with decent and proportionable gesture; these are taught by masters of action (dancing-masters, trainers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When staging, ensure performers are trained in voice modulation and appropriate gestural diction so that words, tone, and movement together excite the intended passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative mood in invocations can be appropriate (not mere command)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Imperative Mood (as used by Homer in invocations) is not always a formal command; it can be a prayer or express pressing necessity or confidence, and thus is allowable in poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject imperative forms in invocations on grammatical grounds alone; consider rhetorical and performative effects and accept imperatives when they convey petition, urgency, or force appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of diction (fundamental units) — definition matters for versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction properly speaking consists of eight parts: Letter, Syllable, Conjunction, Noun, Verb, Article, Case, and Speech; letters divide into vowels, semi-vowels, and mutes; these definitions are the elements from which diction and verse are formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and employ the basic units of language (letters, syllables, conjunctions, etc.) when composing verse and diction; technical differences (vowel, mute, syllable formation) belong to the craft of versification and pronunciation.
